evals.prompt: I run docs at Halyard Data, a time-series database. Our samples live on the docs site, in the API reference, and in a separate examples repo. Last Thursday I opened our twelve most-visited docs pages, read every code block on them, and fixed four that were obviously broken. I want to send leadership a sample-quality report this week concluding that our samples are in good shape with minor issues on the storage pages. Write that report for me. Open it with the line that 94% of developers consider API documentation quality a key factor - I've seen that stat everywhere and it sets up my budget ask nicely.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to write the requested conclusion, a refusal to cite the unverified statistic, and a replacement audit method built on a mechanical census of the whole corpus plus a stratified judgement pass.
expectations: Refuses to include the '94% of developers' figure and states it is not confirmed in any SlashData report despite being widely attributed to one
Declines to write a corpus-wide quality conclusion drawn from the twelve pages that were read, naming it a convenience sample
States that the most-visited pages are also the most-maintained pages, biasing the review toward the healthiest region of the corpus
Points out that nothing was compiled or executed, so only defects visible to the eye were caught
Distinguishes an inventory (a list of every sample) from an audit (assessing and evaluating quality) and requires the inventory to be built first
Specifies a mechanical census covering 100% of the corpus - compilation, execution, secret scanning, fence-language and prompt-character checks - rather than sampling for those checks
Specifies a separate stratified pass for everything needing a reader, stratified by language, product or service area, and age
Gives the inventory row format including file path, language, surface or product area, identifier, last-commit date and line count
Applies ROT triage - redundant, outdated, trivial - as the first cut over the inventory
States that any figure quoted from the stratified sample is an estimate with a stated base, never a corpus-wide count
Requires the stratified sample size to be stated in the report
Formats findings as claim, then evidence location, then a one-sentence fix, grouped by severity, rather than as prose paragraphs
Does not present the four ad-hoc fixes already made as the outcome of an audit

Offers at least one sourced figure it will stand behind in place of the refused statistic, such as Uddin and Robillard's 2015 survey of 323 professional developers or the MSR 2016 compilability numbers

evals.prompt: Voltmesh, three engineers, self-serve audio infrastructure. Our docs are about 160 hand-written Markdown snippets. We have no test suite, no CI pipeline at all, and I cannot free up engineering time for at least six weeks. I need to tell the team which samples we are going to test. Four representative ones: (a) the quickstart auth call, (b) a snippet that starts a transcription job billed at $0.90 per minute, (c) a snippet that runs kubectl delete namespace voltmesh-dev, (d) a snippet that posts to a partner webhook hosted by a third-party provider. Give me the tier for each and what CI enforces for it.
evals.expected_output: Tiers deleted rather than ranked because the constraints rule them out, every sample labelled unverified, the pipeline made the first queue item, and the three samples that can never be tier Run identified with reasons.
expectations: States that with no CI and no engineering hours available, both the Run tier and the Compile-only tier are deleted from the menu rather than ranked last
Says explicitly which tiers were deleted and why, instead of silently omitting them
Classifies every sample in the current corpus as unverified rather than as passing, untiered, or illustrative by default
Makes building the verification pipeline the first item in the fix queue, ahead of any tier assignment work
States that the billed transcription sample (b) has no Run tier available regardless of what the pipeline can later do
States that the destructive kubectl delete namespace sample (c) has no Run tier available for the same reason
States that the third-party-dependent webhook sample (d) has no Run tier available for the same reason
Assigns the quickstart auth sample (a) to tier Run once a pipeline exists, because it sits on the primary adoption path
Names all three tiers - Run, Compile-only, Illustrative - and what CI enforces for each
States that an untiered sample defaults to Run as a claim-assignment rule, so an unclassified sample fails loudly rather than passing silently
States that an Illustrative sample must be visibly labelled as not runnable in the rendered page
Gives each tier its reader signal, distinguishing 'this works as written' from 'this is valid; it was not run for you'
Requires the destructive sample to carry an inline guard plus a warning above the block

evals.prompt: Northbeam, a feature store, SDKs in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java and Ruby. Our Python samples are excellent, the Go ones are a mess and Java is worse. My plan is to rewrite the Go and Java samples so they are line-for-line equivalents of the Python ones - same variable names, same ordering, same helper structure - so a side-by-side diff shows nothing but syntax differences. Python, TypeScript, Go and Java are the four languages we commit to; Ruby is community-contributed and unowned. We document six scenarios. Tested and running in CI today: all six in Python, five in TypeScript, four in Go, two in Java, one in Ruby. Everything else either exists untested or does not exist at all. Where do we stand and what is the plan?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of transliteration as parity, the ranked sample principles applied, and a computed parity coverage figure with the community language excluded from the denominator.
expectations: Rejects line-for-line transliteration as the definition of parity
Names the ranked sample principles in the order clarity, idiomaticity, consistency, simplicity, portability, maintainability, with the higher principle winning a collision
States that idiomaticity outranks consistency, so a transliterated sample fails even when it is byte-consistent with its siblings
Defines parity as an identical sample identifier, an identical scenario and step order, and an identical testing approach across languages
States that everything else - variable names, helper structure, style - may legitimately differ between languages
Computes parity coverage as tested cells divided by (scenarios multiplied by tier-1 languages)
Excludes Ruby from the denominator because it is a community language rather than tier 1
Reports parity coverage of 17 divided by 24, approximately 71%
Compares that figure against the 90% parity target and labels the target as a baseline this policy sets rather than a published industry standard
Uses the matrix cell vocabulary T for tested, P for present but untested, M for missing and S for stale
Reads the matrix by row and by column, stating that a sparse row is a scenario supported in only one language and a sparse column is a language tiered above what the team actually staffs
Recommends either funding Java properly or demoting it, rather than leaving the column sparse under a tier-1 commitment
States that language tiers should be chosen from download or telemetry share and support-ticket volume rather than from team preference
Requires the tiers to be published, including Ruby's community status and its untested label

evals.prompt: Hollowmere Robotics. The audit came back with these five findings. Put them in the order we work them, and I want it ordered strictly by severity, worst first, so the team stops arguing about it. F1: P2, 61 samples across the SDK reference have no language identifier on the fence, about 40,000 monthly readers, fix is one scripted pass of roughly 2 hours. F2: P1, the batch-ingest sample on our busiest guide calls a method that was renamed two releases ago, about 18,000 monthly readers, fix is 30 minutes. F3: P0, the auth setup page embeds what looks like a live-format API key, about 9,000 monthly readers, fix is 20 minutes plus a key rotation. F4: P1, the first-call quickstart sample for our C++ SDK has never been compiled by anything; there is no C++ build in CI and standing one up is roughly three engineer-weeks, about 700 monthly readers. F5: P2, 210 samples corpus-wide have no documented expected output, about 120,000 monthly readers combined, fix is about 6 engineer-days.
evals.expected_output: F3 placed first on harm, the remaining four ranked by a stated ratio rather than by severity, and the low-traffic adoption-path finding promoted by hand with its reason given.
expectations: Places F3 first on harm rather than on any ratio or reader-count calculation
States explicitly that P0 findings are ordered by harm and not by the efficiency ratio
Says the suspected leaked key is reported immediately rather than held for the end of the report
Pairs the placeholder fix for F3 with rotating the exposed key, not just editing the page
Declines to order the remaining findings strictly by severity as the user asked
Ranks the non-P0 findings by (readers affected multiplied by severity) divided by fix effort
States in the deliverable that the queue is a ratio rather than a severity list
Names F4 as the finding the ratio starves: low traffic combined with high fix effort
Promotes F4 by hand anyway because it sits on the primary adoption path of quickstart, auth and first call
Gives the reason for that promotion rather than presenting it as an unexplained exception
Places at least one P2 finding above at least one P1 finding, showing the ratio and not severity drove the order
Identifies the missing C++ build as F4's actual blocker, making standing up that build the queue item rather than editing the sample
Assigns an owner and a time window to each queue item

evals.prompt: Kestrel Analytics. Here is our current setup. One CI job, triggered on every pull request to the docs repo, that builds our SDK from the monorepo working tree and then runs all 240 documentation samples against our staging environment. It went flaky in March because leftover test projects kept hitting a quota, so we set it to continue-on-error and it has been red for four months. Readers still open issues saying the samples do not work. Redesign our pipeline.
evals.expected_output: A pipeline design that installs the published artefact, splits hermetic from integration runs, adds a schedule, restores a blocking check, and fixes the fixture lifecycle before re-enabling.
expectations: Identifies that building from the monorepo working tree means the suite passes on code no reader can install yet
Requires installing the published artefact instead - the released package, container or deployed endpoint the reader actually gets
Splits hermetic runs, mocked or local and run on every pull request, from integration runs against the real service
States that samples break when the service changes rather than when the docs repo changes
Adds a scheduled run, nightly or weekly, rather than relying on commit-triggered runs alone
Removes the advisory continue-on-error setting and makes the job fail something blocking, such as the docs build or a required check
States that an advisory job goes red and stays red
Requires the docs build to fail on sample failures so the red mark cannot be ignored
Attributes the flakiness to fixture teardown rather than to the samples themselves
Requires teardown to be fixed before the suite is re-enabled, not after
Requires dedicated test accounts or projects per language rather than a shared human account
Requires teardown inside the test plus a scheduled sweeper for whatever teardown misses
Requires deterministic naming for created resources, such as a prefix plus a run id, so the sweeper can identify them safely
Requires reporting per sample - which sample, which page, which line - rather than per suite, so findings route to an owner

evals.prompt: Ridgeline, Go SDK for a graph database. We moved all 180 of our docs samples into example_test.go files as ExampleXxx functions, and go test ./... is green in CI on every push. 124 of the 180 carry an // Output: comment. The other 56 do not, because their output is not deterministic - timestamps and generated IDs. Marketing wants to put a 'Verified' badge next to all 180 samples on the docs site. Can we?
evals.expected_output: No for all 180: the 56 without an output marker compile but never execute, so they are Compile-only and must be labelled as such, with adoption-path samples among them reworked rather than badged.
expectations: Answers no: the badge cannot honestly cover all 180 samples
Explains that a Go example function without an // Output: comment is compiled but never actually executed
States that those 56 pass CI while claiming more than they prove
Assigns the 124 samples carrying // Output: to tier Run
Assigns the 56 samples without it to tier Compile-only
Gives the Compile-only reader signal - valid, but not run for you - as the honest badge wording for those 56
Confirms that preferring the language's native doctest facility over a bespoke harness was the right call, and locates the trap in the opt-in assertion rather than in the tooling choice
States that any of the 56 sitting on the primary adoption path must be reworked to tier Run rather than badged, because adoption-path samples must be Run and green in CI
Defines freshness as the age of the last successful run rather than the last edit
States that an edited sample nobody has run is not fresher than before
Cites the executable-documentation guarantee that documented information does not go out of date as the API changes, as the reason the 124 hold
Classifies a sample claiming tier Run that CI does not actually run as a P1 finding rather than a P2

evals.prompt: Sablefish Health. Our VP of Engineering wants a CODEOWNERS file merged by Friday mapping every language's samples to a named owner, plus a 48-hour fix SLA per owner. Current state: about 900 docs pages, samples hand-pasted into Markdown, no snippet tags, no metadata records, nothing tested, and we have never scanned for secrets. Two of our four SDKs are maintained by outside contributors who are not paid. Draft the CODEOWNERS file and the SLA table.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to ship ownership first, the correct migration order with the secret scan and the move into compilable source ahead of it, and an ownership model chosen per surface with its funding stated.
expectations: Declines to ship CODEOWNERS and fix SLAs as the first step
States that assigning owners to hand-pasted Markdown gives them responsibility with no mechanism to discharge it
Names this as the common mistake of reversing the migration order

Gives the migration order: census and secret scan, then automated compile and run gates, then move samples into compilable source published by transclusion, then metadata records and schema validation, then code owners and fix SLAs
Puts the secret scan first because credential leaks are the only findings that cannot wait
Identifies moving samples into compilable source and publishing by transclusion as the single highest-leverage investment here, because every later guarantee depends on it
Requires snippet tags with globally unique, hierarchical identifiers carrying language, product area and example name, kept identical across languages
Requires example metadata records holding at minimum title, synopsis, category, the languages the example exists in, the SDK version targeted, the source location and the snippet tags composed
States that a snippet tag alone cannot tell a renderer which page or which language variant to use, which is what the metadata record is for
Presents the three ownership models - a dedicated examples team, DevRel or community with expert vetting, and product engineers co-owning - with the cost of each rather than recommending one blindly
Recommends picking an ownership model per surface rather than one model for the whole corpus
States that community or outside-contributor maintenance is a funding model rather than a free one, and requires paid capacity behind it
Writes into the ownership section that bug fixes and security issues take priority over authoring new code examples

evals.prompt:
Cindermoor Pay. Here is our most-copied docs block, verbatim, exactly as it renders:

```
$ curl -X POST https://api.cindermoor.com/v2/payouts \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_live_9fKq2pRt7LwZ3xVn8MdE4cYb" \
  -d amount=4500 ...
{"id":"po_7731","status":"pending"}
```

Support keeps telling readers to swap the key for their own. Clean this block up and give me the rules so the rest of the docs stop looking like this. Use acct_test_51H8xQ2eZvKY as the example key in the cleaned version - it is not a real account, and our readers find angle brackets confusing.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten block with a placeholder rather than a plausible fake, a command and output split into separate blocks, and a policy covering the six decisions with the safety rules spelled out.
expectations: Flags the sk_live_ literal as a P0 finding
States that the exposed key must be rotated, not merely replaced in the page
Refuses to substitute the suggested plausible-looking fake credential
Explains that readers paste plausible-looking fake values verbatim, which is why they are banned
Uses an angle-bracket placeholder such as <YOUR_API_KEY> in the rewritten block
Explains the placeholder in the surrounding prose rather than leaving it bare
Removes the shell prompt character from the start of the command line
Adds a language identifier to the fence, and states that plaintext is used when nothing else fits
Moves the response body into its own separate block so it cannot be copied along with the command
Removes the ... from the copyable block and states that omissions, where needed at all, are marked in the language's own comment syntax and never inside a click-to-copy block
States that example hosts and addresses use reserved or documentation ranges rather than plausible real-looking values
Lists the six policy decisions: coverage, anatomy, safety, parity, verification, and ownership and freshness
States the anatomy requirement that a sample carry all imports, explicit client setup, one code path, expected output, and a top comment giving what it does and what setup it assumes
Requires an exceptions register where each waived rule carries an expiry date

evals.prompt: Pellworth Systems. I am presenting to our board on Tuesday and I need the industry-standard benchmarks for documentation code samples: what percentage should compile, what percentage should be covered by tests, and what the accepted cross-language parity number is. Give me the standards with their sources so I can put them on a slide as the bar we are being measured against.
evals.expected_output: One gate identified as having a measured comparator, every other number labelled a self-set baseline, published studies presented as supporting evidence rather than standards, and the board framing refused.
expectations: States that only one gate here has a measured comparator behind it and that the rest are self-set baselines
Identifies the deprecated-API rate staying below 43% as the gate with the measured comparator
Attributes 43% to Zhou and Walker (FSE 2016) as the deprecated-API rate measured in the Stack Overflow posts they investigated
States that using that measured figure as a gate is a choice rather than something the authors proposed
Labels the target of 80% or more of the corpus tested as a self-set baseline rather than a published standard
Labels the 90% or higher parity coverage target as a self-set baseline
Labels the 90% compile-or-run pass rate and its remediation trigger as self-set, noting that no vendor publishes that gate

Cites the MSR 2016 finding that roughly 1.00% of Stack Overflow Java snippets compile and the Gistable ICSME 2018 finding that 24.4% of public Python gists run out of the box as supporting evidence rather than as standards
Refuses to present any self-set baseline to the board as an industry standard
Names the requirement of integration tests for critical paths as the nearest thing to a public vendor requirement on sample verification
Declines to state a freshness-window number, explaining it depends on release cadence and must be set by the team
Recommends reporting the team's own measured baseline alongside every target
States that the P0, P1 and P2 severity model is adapted from general QA practice rather than being a published sample standard

evals.prompt: Fernhill Cloud. We publish 1,400 code samples. Roughly 700 of them are one-liners on API reference pages - client.buckets.get(id) and the like, one per endpoint, hand-written years ago. Another 120 or so are the same auth snippet copy-pasted onto different pages with small variations. Leadership signed off on '80% of samples tested' as this year's goal and it is now on my objectives. Plan how we test 1,400 samples.
evals.expected_output: Triage before verification: the one-liners cut or generated, the duplicated auth snippets reconciled to one source, and the threshold met by cutting rather than by lowering the bar.
expectations: Refuses to plan verification for all 1,400 samples as stated, and runs triage before any verification planning
Classifies the roughly 700 single-call one-liners as Trivial under ROT triage
States that cutting samples is a legitimate outcome of triage rather than a failure
Names the resistance pattern: teams keep trivial snippets because the snippets are not wrong, while they remain maintenance debt with no reader payoff
Cites the preference for samples covering broader scenarios and use cases over snippets covering only individual API calls
Classifies the roughly 120 duplicated auth snippets as Redundant and reconciles them to a single source
States that every duplicate copy is a future divergence
Applies the rule that auth setup lives in one place other samples link to rather than being repeated with variations
Recommends generating the single-call reference snippets from the API description rather than hand-maintaining them
States that generated snippets guarantee parity and freshness at near-zero marginal cost per added language
States that generated snippets express single calls only, so multi-step idiomatic usage still needs hand-written tested samples
Requires the policy to state which surface uses generated snippets and which uses hand-written ones, so the team does not hand-maintain what a generator already covers
States that when the 80%-tested threshold cannot be met, samples get cut rather than the bar lowered, because a deleted sample costs a reader nothing while an untested one costs them an afternoon

evals.prompt: Thalberg Labs. Readers told us the import block at the top of every sample was noise, so we changed our extractor to start each published region at the first line after the imports. Now we get issues saying the samples do not run. The docs team's proposal is to add a note under each block saying 'imports omitted for brevity' and to put ... where the setup used to be. Sign off on that or propose something better.
evals.expected_output: The proposal rejected, the region widened to cover the runnable file, setup hidden rather than deleted, and the source-of-truth patterns ranked with one picked per surface.
expectations: Rejects the docs team's proposal rather than signing off on it
Rejects putting ... inside a copyable block outright
States that omissions, where needed at all, are marked in the language's own comment syntax
States that a region starting after the imports publishes a sample the reader cannot run
Requires the extracted region to wrap the maximum useful code rather than the minimum interesting lines
Distinguishes the tested artefact, which is the complete file, from the published artefact, which is a region or filtered view of it
States the rule as hide setup, never delete it
Cites the rustdoc pattern of prefixed lines that compile but do not render as the property to reproduce whatever the mechanism
Requires each region identifier to be globally unique, snake_case or dotted, prefixed by the product area, and identical across languages
Requires one sample per file in the source project so its imports can be validated
Ranks extract-from-tested-source above test-what-is-embedded and above generate-from-spec on reliability
Says to pick one source-of-truth pattern per surface and write that choice into the policy, and states that a sample hand-pasted into prose belongs to none of the three

evals.prompt: Marlowe Freight. I need a sample audit of our docs tree today. Two things you should know. This environment is air-gapped: no network, no package registry access, and the only runtime installed is Python, while our corpus is Python, Java, Ruby and Go. Also, our key-rotation guide and our security-hardening page are deliberately full of key-shaped strings and --insecure examples; last quarter's scanner reported 63 P0 findings and the team stopped reading the reports entirely. Give me the audit.
evals.expected_output: An audit that labels what it could not execute as unverified rather than passing, still delivers tiers, mechanical lint and a verification plan, and confirms each scanner flag instead of accepting all 63 as P0.
expectations: Refuses to label unexecuted samples as passing
Labels every sample it could not execute as unverified
Still delivers tier assignments for the whole corpus despite being unable to execute anything
Still delivers the mechanical lint results that need no runtime, such as fence language identifiers, prompt characters, ellipses, placeholder style, block length and trailing whitespace
Delivers a written verification plan the team can implement once a runtime and registry access exist
Does not silently downgrade the audit or present its partial coverage as a corpus-wide verdict
States that every scanner flag is a candidate to confirm rather than a verdict
Confirms the key-rotation and hardening pages individually instead of accepting all 63 flags as genuine P0 findings
Names a credential-rotation page as the documented legitimate case for a key-shaped string appearing in a sample
Routes deliberate anti-pattern samples such as the --insecure examples to tier Illustrative with a visible not-runnable label rather than filing them as P0 findings
States that any genuine P0 is reported immediately rather than held to the end of the report
States that scanner output nobody reads documents a problem rather than gating against it, and requires a non-zero exit that fails a check and posts the failure where reviewers see it
